job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Uma Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I wake up in a rented flat in Headingley that I share with my friend Lena, and I cycle to a credit union office in the middle of Leeds. I'm a loans operations analyst, so I check applications, chase missing payslips and flag odd cases to the senior underwriter. Lunch is usually at my desk with a podcast, and in the evening I either go to a pottery class or call my little sister Ilka, who's 16 and panicking about exams.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how did you land that job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I studied economics and finance and got a good result. I did a three-month internship at a building society in my third year, which I think is what got me noticed. Mum runs a small cleaning business and can help me out in a bad month, but I'm careful about asking, and I still owe loans of about 13 thousand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's useful for the boring bits and nothing more. I'd tell Lena that I use an assistant now and then to summarise long emails, but I check every output. Online I'd probably just roll my eyes at the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my life carries on and that's quite a relief. Credit unions are member-owned and move slowly, and my contract is permanent. I'm paying off loans through my payslip, not out of fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at the credit union and try to get on the member-lending team in a year or so. I'd put 200 a month into a savings account and carry on with my pottery class. I'd also keep trying the assistant for small jobs, because it's handy for drafting letters to members.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. It's nice to picture a world where I can just plan my next promotion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound calm. Is there nothing about the world as it is that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There is. Rents are crazy and Lena and I have talked about moving to a cheaper area. And I worry about Mum's business, because cleaning contracts get cut when firms tighten up. But those are old worries, not AI ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you help Mum if the business had a bad year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd send her 150 a month from my pay and cut my pottery and my weekend trips. It would hurt, but I'd rather that than see her take on another overnight contract.

say: I'd say AI is **useful** for boring jobs and nothing more.
I'd admit I use an assistant for **summaries** but check every output.
think: My life carries on, which is a **relief**, because my permanent contract feels safe.
I pay the loans through my **payslip** without fear.
do: Keep working and try to move to the **member-lending** team within a year.
Put **200 a month** into savings and keep the pottery class.
Keep using the assistant to draft **letters** to members.
feel: **Calm**, because the world stays predictable enough to plan the next promotion.
S0.quote: Credit unions are member-owned and move slowly, and my contract is permanent.
fieldNote: Uma's calm is based on a **permanent contract** and a slow, member-owned employer.
She still carries two old worries: city rents and her mother's cleaning contracts.
Uses AI lightly and checks it, matching her steady profile.

steps.text: Apply for the member-lending team at the credit union within a year
Pay 200 a month into a savings account
Use the assistant to draft member letters and check each one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we should be told early what the software will do, and who checks it. Online I'd back calls for workers to have a say in how it's introduced, because my first worry is firms using it as an excuse to freeze hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think loan checking is exactly the kind of work that gets taken first, ticking documents and spotting missing figures. The credit union is kind, but even kind employers watch the budget. I think they'll hire fewer analysts and ask the rest to do more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for an evening data analysis course at the local college, about 40 a week, so I can move toward underwriting, which is judgement. I'd also ask the senior underwriter, Gemma, if I can sit in on the hard cases. And I'd join the finance workers' union branch, partly for the training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a motivated way. I feel like I have some control, as long as I move early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said they'd hire fewer analysts. What would you do if you were one of the ones they let go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to the union for advice and apply to the other credit unions and the local council. I'd also lean on Mum for a month or two of rent. I wouldn't hide it, because hiding it is what makes people ashamed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust the software at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I could see how it reached a decision, and if a person was named as responsible. At the moment, the vendor says it's accurate, but I'd want the figures for my own members.

say: I'd ask to be told **early** what the software will do and who checks it.
I'd back worker **voice** in how firms bring it in.
think: Loan checking is exactly the kind of **thinking work** that gets taken first.
I expect fewer analysts and **more work** for those who stay.
do: Sign up for an evening **data course** at about 40 a week.
Ask the senior underwriter, Gemma, to let me sit in on hard **cases**.
feel: **Anxious**, but motivated, since there is some control if I move early.
S1.quote: The credit union is kind, but even kind employers watch the budget.
fieldNote: Uma reads her own role as **exposed**, yet she responds with training and union membership.
She wants named human responsibility for software decisions.
Open to the tools, but only with transparency.

steps.text: Enrol in the evening data analysis course at the local college
Join the finance workers' union branch this spring
Sit in on hard loan cases with underwriter Gemma

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need a meeting about what happens to every junior role, and I'd say it politely but firmly. Online I'd push for emergency public support, a pause in hiring cuts and a say for workers. Two years is just not enough for governments or families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my job goes inside a year or two. Everything I do is reading, checking and flagging, which is what the machine does best. I'd be among the first to be told that the branch is merging roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending the first week and save about 600 a month, since I'd have fewer weeks before the money gets tight. I'd go to the union and push for a retraining income. I'd also look for hands-on work as a bridge, perhaps in my mum's cleaning business or a care role, since robots for hands are about three years behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. I'd feel angry at the people who knew, and sad for Ilka, who's about to choose what to study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned working in your mum's business. What would that be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Odd, to be honest. I'd be washing offices for the same people I'd have been approving loans for. But Mum would be happy to have me, and it keeps my hands busy while I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister, Ilka?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't panic and don't pick a degree just for the salary. I'd tell her to learn something with people in it, like teaching or nursing, and to keep her options open.

say: I'd call a **meeting** about what happens to every junior role.
I'd push for emergency public **support** and a pause on cuts.
think: My job could go within **a year or two**, since I read, check and flag all day.
I'd be among the **first** told that roles are merging.
do: Cut spending and save about **600 a month** from the first week.
Ask the union for a **retraining income**.
Take **hands-on** bridge work, maybe in Mum's cleaning business or a care role.
feel: **Alarmed**, angry at people who knew, and sad for my sister Ilka.
S2.quote: I'd be washing offices for the same people I'd have been approving loans for.
fieldNote: Uma expects the job to go **within two years** and plans a bridge.
The cleaning business is a family safety net, not a fantasy.
Her concern for her sister, Ilka, shows what is really at stake.

steps.text: Cut weekend trips and save about 600 a month
Move savings into a separate account for six months of rent
Ask the union about a retraining income and join its campaign
Work shifts in my mum's cleaning business while searching

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is a window and we should use it. Online I'd push for retraining funds, a shorter working week and worker representation, and I'd remind people that governments move slowly unless they're pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm anxious but not shaken. In five years I'd be 27, with a few years' experience and a chance to move into something judgement-heavy. The risk is that every other junior is doing the same thing at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the data course now and the underwriting exam in the second year. I'd save about 400 a month, since time lets me build a decent cushion. I'd also use the AI tools much more, so I'm the person on the team who knows how to check them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier than the two-year world. Five years feels like enough time to bend my path without breaking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be the one who checks the tools. What does that look like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be the person who reads the machine's loan decisions and signs off or sends back the odd ones. It's less typing and more judgement, and members would still want a human voice when they've been refused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change compared with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lets me plan instead of just reacting. With two years I'm selling a bike and calling the union. With five I can study and save. I can still see my flatmate Lena, and Ilka gets to finish school before things change.

say: I'd say five years is a **window** and we should use it.
I'd push for retraining funds and **worker** representation.
think: I'm anxious but not **shaken**, since I'd be 27 with real experience.
The risk is every other **junior** moving the same way at the same time.
do: Take the data course now and the **underwriting exam** in the second year.
Save about **400 a month** to build a decent cushion.
Use AI tools more so I become the **checker** on my team.
feel: **Steadier** than the two-year world, with time to bend my path without breaking it.
S3.quote: With two years I'm selling a bike and calling the union. With five I can study and save.
fieldNote: Time lets Uma shift from **survival** to positioning herself as the human checker.
Concern for the crowd of other juniors shows realism, not panic.
Her plan depends on funded retraining being real.

steps.text: Take the underwriting exam in the second year
Save 400 a month into a separate account
Review the software's loan decisions and become the team's checker

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to build proper public support. Online I'd talk about retraining and a fair share of the gains, and I'd probably join some campaign group, because there's time to make a difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fairly relaxed. By 2036 I'd be 32, probably a senior underwriter or in a different field, with savings and a flat of my own. Still, a decade can change a lot and I wouldn't want to coast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep up with the technology, because that's the habit that matters, and I'd move into a role with more members and fewer forms. I'd save about 300 a month for a deposit. I'd also help Ilka through university and pick a campaign group to give a few hours a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly relaxed, though never fully. Ten years feels like a decent amount of room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd give time to a campaign group. What kind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably one about fair pay and retraining for people whose jobs shift. I've seen what happens to Mum's cleaners when a contract goes, and I want a safety net that doesn't depend on luck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you less relaxed in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If nothing happened in the first three or four years. If politicians waited until the end, we'd be back to the two-year panic with fewer years left.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a real chance to build public support.
I'd talk about **retraining** and a fair share of the gains.
think: By 2036 I'd be **32**, maybe a senior underwriter, fairly relaxed.
I wouldn't want to **coast**, since a decade can change a lot.
do: Keep up with the **technology** and move to a members-facing role.
Save **300 a month** towards a deposit.
Help my sister Ilka through **university** and join a campaign group.
feel: **Relaxed**, though never fully, with a decent amount of room.
S4.quote: If politicians waited until the end, we'd be back to the two-year panic with fewer years left.
fieldNote: Uma's relaxed tone is conditional on **early public action**.
She links her campaign interest to what she has seen happen to her mother's cleaners.
The sister, Ilka, appears again as a life plan.

steps.text: Move into a member-facing lending role with fewer forms
Save 300 a month towards a flat deposit
Help Ilka with university costs and choosing a degree
Give a few hours a month to a retraining campaign group

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time for the public side of things to catch up. What would help is real, fast public support: a retraining income, rent help and a say for workers in how firms bring in the technology. Also a job guarantee in the care and public sectors would calm a lot of people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much I think about my sister. I want her to choose a degree without having to guess what a machine can do. I'd tell any politician that the young people are the ones this will land on, and we're the ones with the least say.

headlineQuote: I'd tell any politician that the young people are the ones this will land on, and we're the ones with the least say.
portrait: Uma, 22, is a **loans analyst** at a member-owned credit union in Leeds, with a permanent contract.
She shares a flat, owes about **13 thousand** and has some savings, with her mum's help in a pinch.
Progressive and steady, she tries tools but wants rules, **worker voice** and public support.
She moves from calm in the plateau world to alarmed at two years, with a **bridge** into hands-on work.
Her little sister Ilka and her mum's cleaning business shape most of her choices.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because there is no time for public support or retraining to be built.
whatWouldHelp: Fast public **support**: a retraining income, rent help and a say for workers in how firms bring in AI.
